by Colin Barrow (Author) Format: Paperback 

 5.0 5.0 out of 5 stars (8) 

 Explore the gripping intersection of war history and culinary legacy. The liberation of Paris was not the end of the war in France. Many combatants, French citizens, and Resistance fighters were yet to endure much. Remarkably, the daily death toll after D-Day was twice as high as before. Yet amidst these tragedies, a unique facet of history emerged: the role of the Michelin Guide. The Allies used the 1939 guide to navigate French regions, identifying hotels to accommodate battle-weary troops or to serve as headquarters. Astonishingly, over 100 of these great restaurants remain. From the Grand Hôtel de Cabourg near Sword Beach to La Palme d’Or along the Côte d'Azur, these historic venues offer a window into the past. Operation Valkyrie, led by von Stauffenberg on July 20, 1944, to assassinate Hitler, failed. But in Paris the plot was so well advanced that they had already arrested most of the Nazi SS officers before the coup unravelled when it was revealed Hitler survived. Consequently, the plotters released their captives. In a bizarre twist the SS officers and their captors shared a meal at the Hôtel Majestic (now renamed as The Peninsula Paris), before despatching the plotters back to their executions in Germany. Colin was educated at Sandhurst, earned an MBA from Cranfield, and attended the MA War Studies course at King’s College London, as well as the Associate MA Military History course at Buckingham University. He is a Fellow of the Royal Society of Arts. His books have been published by the Economist, BBC, Sunday Times, The Telegraph, John Wiley (Dummies series), and Kogan Page, among others, and have been translated into numerous languages.

## Colin Barrow

...

5 out of 5 stars

##### Michelin dining with historical purpose - enjoy!

Reviewed in the United Kingdom on 20 April 2025

Format: Kindle Edition

Verified Purchase

...

A new book intertwines two historical perspectives that, at first sight seem unusual bedfellows: the emancipation of France and the resilience of the recommendations of the Michelin Guide. The revelation of the role played by the Guide in the military endeavour only seems obvious with hindsight. The introduction alone is sufficient to titillate the appetite for the succeeding chapters. What brings the theme right up to date is the resilience of the Michelin network of places to enjoy fine dining and relaxation.

The book reveals impressive detail of the numerous code-named operations involved in eventual emancipation of France and the author’s assurance of the existence of each and every Michelin establishment still in operation since 1939.

Although the modern relevance of the once famous maps and instructions for tire repair and replacement has diminished, the relevance of listings of hotels and restaurants certainly has not.

This is a seriously informative yet entertaining read. I thoroughly enjoyed it.

## Description
Men Who Have Made the Empire is a 1899 volume of short biographies describing acts of bravery and integrity by twelve Englishmen. Similar to the American book Profiles in Courage by John F. Kennedy, the book profiles explorers, businessmen and statemen who defied the odds and built the largest Empire in human history. The book was written in 1899 and is one of several last examples of 'Great Man' histories prior to the rise of the Annales School and a growing aversion to imperialism in the 20th Century.

# Go Like Hell: Ford, Ferrari, and Their Battle for Speed and Glory at Le Mans 

 by A. J. Baime (Author) Format: Paperback 

 4.7 4.7 out of 5 stars (3,446) 

 As told in the film Ford v. Ferrari, Go Like Hell transports readers to a risk-filled, glorious time in this brilliant portrait of a rivalry between two industrialists, the cars they built, and the "pilots" who would drive them to victory, or doom. By the early 1960s, the Ford Motor Company, built to bring automobile transportation to the masses, was falling behind. Young Henry Ford II, who had taken the reins of his grandfather's company with little business experience to speak of, knew he had to do something to shake things up. Baby boomers were taking to the road in droves, looking for speed not safety, style not comfort. Meanwhile, Enzo Ferrari, whose cars epitomized style, lorded it over the European racing scene. He crafted beautiful sports cars, "science fiction on wheels," but was also called "the Assassin" because so many drivers perished while racing them. Go Like Hell tells the remarkable story of how Henry Ford II, with the help of a young visionary named Lee Iacocca and a former racing champion turned engineer, Carroll Shelby, concocted a scheme to reinvent the Ford company. They would enter the high-stakes world of European car racing, where an adventurous few threw safety and sanity to the wind. They would design, build, and race a car that could beat Ferrari at his own game at the most prestigious and brutal race in the world, something no American car had ever done.

# The Limit: Life and Death in Formula One's Most Dangerous Era 

 by Michael Cannell (Author) Format: Kindle Edition 

| 4.4 4.4 out of 5 stars (480) |
| --- |

10 September 1961: at the boomerang-shaped racetrack at Monza, in northern Italy, half a dozen teams are preparing for the Italian Grand Prix. It is the biggest race anyone can remember. Phil Hill - the first American to break into the top ranks of European racing - and his Ferrari teammate, Count Wolfgang von Trips - a German nobleman with a movie-star manner - face each another in a race that will decide the winner of the Formula One drivers' championship. By the day's end, one man will clinch that prize. The other will perish face down on the track. In The Limit, Michael Cannell tells the thrilling story of two parallel lives that come together in tragedy on a hot late-summer afternoon. He charts their careers from childhood and adolescence lived in the shadow of world war; through their gruelling experiences in such deadly road races as the Mille Miglia and the 24 Hours of Le Mans; to their coming of age in the hothouse atmosphere of Enzo Ferrari's Formula One team of the late 1950s. The quiet and self-contained Hill was a pathological worrier who vomited before a race and enjoyed Bartok and Shostakovich - rather than Campari and debauchery - thereafter; the dashing von Trips lived life as fast as he drove his 'sharknose' Ferrari, and yearned to inspire a nation fractured and traumatized by war. Both men strove to attain the perfect balance of speed and control that drivers called 'the limit': to drive under that limit was to run the risk of failure; to go beyond it was to dice with death. The Limit is a vivid and atmospheric recreation of a lost world of seductive glamour and ever-present danger. Michael Cannell tells a moving and unforgettable tale of high speed and burning rivalry - and of young lives lived in the shadow of oblivion.
